title: Decision trees: classification with questions
intro: A decision tree sorts data with yes/no questions. No formulas, no coefficients — just questions like “is income below $2,500?”. That makes trees the most interpretable model in scikit-learn, and at the same time the textbook example of overfitting when you let them grow unchecked.
keyPoints: A tree splits the data with yes/no questions (feature + threshold) until its leaves are pure: each leaf predicts one class.
Each split picks the feature + threshold that reduces impurity the most — measured with Gini or entropy.
Trees need no scaling and capture non-linear patterns — but without a brake they grow themselves into overfitting.
Brakes: max_depth, min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf — see the topic Bias-variance tradeoff.

blocks.html: A decision tree classifies by sorting data with questions. Every internal node asks one question of the form “is feature \( x_j \) smaller than threshold \( t \)?”, and the two answers (“yes” left, “no” right) lead to the next question. At the bottom sit the leaves: there the final verdict falls — the majority class of the training samples in that leaf.

For a loan application the tree might read: “is income $2,500 or higher?” — yes → “is debt below $500?” — yes → leaf approved. A new application falls from top to bottom and ends up in exactly one leaf. You can literally explain that path to a customer — with logistic regression (a weighted sum of features) it already feels far more abstract, and with an RBF SVM it is practically impossible.

The tree predicts with axis-aligned splits: every question cuts along one feature axis (“below \( t \)?”). The decision boundary is therefore a composition of straight lines — non-linear as a whole, but built from simple pieces. See the topic Linear decision boundaries for the contrast with the single straight line.

sections.title: Splitting: where do you cut the data?

blocks.html: The central building block is the split: pick one feature \( x_j \) and one threshold \( t \), and divide the samples into two groups — \( x_j \le t \) left and \( x_j > t \) right. scikit-learn effectively tries every (feature, threshold) combination and keeps the split that lays the two groups apart most cleanly: one side mostly positives, the other mostly negatives.

That search is greedy and top-down (the CART algorithm): start at the root with all data, pick the single best split, apply the same step to both halves, and so on. “Greedy” means each split picks only what is best now, without lookahead — the tree cannot come back on an earlier choice. In practice that works surprisingly well.
Quick demo with eight samples and two features (income and age): at the root, 3 approved (✓) and 5 rejected (✗) applications are mixed.

Note that one split rarely suffices: after “income ≤ 2500” the left side still mixes ✓ and ✗. So the tree grows: every impure child gets its own new split, with a different feature or threshold — until every leaf is pure or a stopping condition (depth, minimum samples) kicks in.

“Pure” needs to be measurable. Suppose the fraction of positives in a node is \( p \) (and \( 1-p \) negatives). There are two standard impurity measures — both 0 for a pure node (\( p = 0 \) or \( p = 1 \)) and maximal for a 50/50 mix:

blocks.label: Gini impurity
blocks.caption: The probability that two random samples from the node have different classes. Max 0.5 at p = 0.5 — the scikit-learn default.

blocks.label: Entropy
blocks.caption: The ‘chaos’ in bits; max 1 at p = 0.5. Virtually identical in shape to Gini — in practice the choice hardly matters.

blocks.title: Gini and entropy as a function of p
blocks.subtitle: Drag the slider: at p = 0 or 1 the node is pure (both measures 0), at p = 0.5 the mixture is maximal. The live metrics follow along.

blocks.html: So how does the tree pick the best split? It looks for the split that minimises the weighted average impurity of the children — or equivalently, the one that reduces impurity the most (the information gain). “Weighted” is essential: a split that puts 99% of the samples into one pure child and 1% into one very dirty child need not beat a split that cleans up both halves substantially.

Worked out for the split “income ≤ 2500” from the demo (\( p \) = fraction ✓ per group). The root has \( p = 3/8 = 0{,}375 \), so \( G = 2 \cdot 0{,}375 \cdot 0{,}625 = 0{,}469 \). The left child has \( n_L = 6 \) with \( p_L = 1/6 \): \( G_L = 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{6} \cdot \tfrac{5}{6} = 0{,}278 \). The right child has \( n_R = 2 \) with \( p_R = 1 \): pure, \( G_R = 0 \). The weighted child impurity is \( \tfrac{6}{8} \cdot 0{,}278 + \tfrac{2}{8} \cdot 0 = 0{,}208 \) — a hefty drop from 0.469.

In scikit-learn you pick the measure with criterion: DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="gini") or criterion="entropy". Gini is the default. In practice both yield virtually the same trees — the thresholds they settle on lie so close together that it is not worth agonising over.

sections.title: When does the tree stop? The overfit trap

blocks.html: Growing without limit is dangerous. A tree that continues until every leaf is pure always reaches 100% training accuracy — because eventually each leaf holds exactly one sample, which it of course predicts correctly. But that is no longer learning, that is memorising the training data: exactly the overfitting from the topic What is machine learning?, now in its most extreme form.
scikit-learn therefore ships stopping brakes — called pre-pruning, because they trim the tree during growth:

rows: the number of questions below the root
a node with fewer samples will not split
every leaf keeps at least n samples
prediction is a majority over enough data
a hard cap on model size

blocks.html: The brakes shift the balance between bias (too flat → systematically off target) and variance (too deep → different training set, different tree). How to explain and tune that balance is the topic Bias-variance tradeoff — for trees, max_depth is the textbook knob.

The workflow is exactly the standard trio from the topic Supervised learning: fit, predict, score. No scaler, no pipeline needed — thresholds are scale-independent. The example below trains one unrestricted tree and one braked tree on the breast-cancer dataset and compares train and test scores:

blocks.caption: unrestricted vs. pruned tree on breast_cancer
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# 1) tree without a brake: grows until every leaf is pure
tree_free = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42)
tree_free.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

# 2) tree with a brake: at most 3 questions deep
tree_pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
tree_pruned.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print('unrestricted: train', round(tree_free.score(X_tr, y_tr), 3),
      '| test', round(tree_free.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
print('max_depth=3 : train', round(tree_pruned.score(X_tr, y_tr), 3),
      '| test', round(tree_pruned.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
print('leaves:', tree_free.get_n_leaves(), 'vs',
      tree_pruned.get_n_leaves())

blocks.html: The typical picture: the unrestricted tree sits at 100% training accuracy and loses almost five percentage points on the test set — a classic variance signal. The pruned tree scores slightly lower on train but here better on test (0.958 vs 0.951), with half the number of leaves (8 vs 16). That is the bias-variance balance in one line of output.

blocks.caption: reading the tree as human rules
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

data = load_breast_cancer()
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(
    data.data, data.target)

# the first two questions of the tree, with the class per leaf
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=data.feature_names,
                  max_depth=2))

blocks.html: export_text shows the tree as rules — exactly the form you can put in front of a domain expert (“does it make sense that these two measurements almost settle the whole decision?”). For a genuine why discussion this is gold; no other model in scikit-learn is this transparent.

sections.title: Strengths and weaknesses in one table

blocks.html: When do you pick a tree, and when rather logistic regression or an SVM? The honest trade-off:

rows: small data change → very different tree (high variance)
a single tree usually loses to ensembles (random forest)

blocks.html: The big weakness — high variance — is at the same time the door to what follows: many random, slightly different trees average away that noise (random forests, outside the scope of this course). First the fundamental framework: the topic Bias-variance tradeoff shows why “a single tree is fickle” and “the average of many trees is not” are two sides of the same mathematics.
